title: How sailors measured speed with a knotted rope
description:
Throw a wooden board off the stern: it grips the water while the ship sails on, pulling line off a reel. Turn a 28-second sandglass and count the knots that run out. The knots are 47 feet 3 inches apart, which is how far a ship doing one nautical mile an hour (6,080 feet) moves in 28 seconds, so the count is the speed: 7 knots is 7 nautical miles an hour. Log speed and heading every hour and you can plot where you are (dead reckoning), until a current you can't see drags you off: 1 knot of current is 24 miles in a day. That's why speed at sea and in the air is still measured in knots.

Numbers checked in code: knot spacing from the 6,080-foot Admiralty mile and a 28-second glass (47.29 ft), 100,000 simulated casts, and the examples. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_(unit), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_log, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_reckoning.

social_caption: Sailors counted knots on a rope for 28 seconds and got their speed. Here's why the spacing makes the count come out exactly right.
facts_checked: Before the mid-19th century, speed was measured with a chip log: knots 47 ft 3 in (14.4018 m) apart, timed with a 28-second sand-glass (30 s earlier), giving 1.85166 km/h per knot, within 0.02% of today's 1.852 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_(unit))
Admiralty nautical mile 6,080 ft; knot = one nautical mile per hour, used at sea and in aviation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_(unit))

The log is dropped off the stern, acts as a drogue, and the sailor counts the knots passing through his hands in a fixed time; first printed description William Bourne 1574 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_log)
Dead reckoning: position from a previous fix plus speed, heading and elapsed time; errors compound over distance; currents are not accounted for (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_reckoning)
6,080 ft x 28/3600 = 47.29 ft = 47 ft 3 in to the inch; 100,000 simulated casts: knots counted = speed in knots; 7 x 4 = 28 miles; 1 knot x 24 h = 24 miles (verify.py)

beats.say: Count knots on a rope for 28 seconds: that's your speed.
No GPS, no land in sight. The rope does the math.
Mid-Atlantic, 400 years ago. Where are you?
Step 1: throw a wooden board off the back. It grips the water and pulls rope off a reel.
Step 2: turn a 28 second sandglass and count the knots that slip out. 7.
The knots sit 47 feet 3 inches apart: how far one nautical mile an hour goes in 28 seconds. So 7 knots means 7 nautical miles an hour.
Step 3: log it every hour. 7 knots, west, for 4 hours: 28 miles west of your last fix.
Uh-oh: a current you can't see. Just 1 knot puts you 24 miles off in a day.
That rope is why ships and planes still measure speed in knots.
